title: Query Execution Plans and Cost Concepts
learningObjectives: Explain why a database optimizer creates an execution plan.
Read a basic SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN result.
Distinguish a table scan from an indexed search.
Explain why plan text can vary with engine versions and statistics.
Use result correctness and plan evidence together when tuning a query.

understand.concept: A query execution plan describes how the database intends to obtain the requested rows. The optimizer compares candidate access paths and chooses one using estimates about data, indexes and operation costs.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding a plan helps explain why a query reads many rows, uses an index, sorts intermediate results or performs repeated lookups.
understand.analogy: A delivery planner chooses a route based on road conditions and destination locations.
understand.analogyLimit: An execution plan is an estimate or strategy description, not a guaranteed elapsed time. Actual performance also depends on cache state, concurrency, storage and data volume.

explain.narrative:
## Query planning
The optimizer transforms a declarative SQL request into an execution strategy. Depending on the engine, a plan can include scans, index lookups, joins, sorts, aggregates and temporary structures.

## SQLite plan inspection
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN gives a high-level description of SQLite's chosen strategy. A SCAN indicates that rows are visited through a scan; SEARCH indicates that a constraint is used to narrow access. Exact plan text can change with SQLite versions, indexes and statistics.

## Cost and correctness
The optimizer estimates work; it does not know every runtime condition. Always verify that a rewritten query returns the same rows and values, then measure representative workloads. A plan that uses an index is not automatically faster for every data distribution.

examples.title: Create an order table with a primary key
examples.code: CREATE TABLE perf22_orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_code TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, amount INTEGER NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates an order table. The INTEGER PRIMARY KEY gives SQLite an indexed row identifier that can support direct key lookups.

examples.title: Generate a reproducible order set
examples.code: WITH RECURSIVE seq(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < 100) INSERT INTO perf22_orders SELECT n, 'C-' || printf('%03d', n % 20), CASE WHEN n % 10 = 0 THEN 'review' ELSE 'paid' END, n * 5 FROM seq;
examples.explanation: Creates 100 rows with a predictable distribution: ten review orders and ninety paid orders. The sample is useful for demonstrating access paths, not for production benchmarking.

examples.title: Inspect a primary-key lookup plan
examples.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT status, amount FROM perf22_orders WHERE order_id = 50;
examples.expectedOutput: Plan uses an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY search
examples.explanation: The primary-key equality predicate allows SQLite to locate the row directly through the rowid alias. The exact plan wording is version-dependent.

examples.title: Return the requested order
examples.code: SELECT order_id, status, amount FROM perf22_orders WHERE order_id = 50;
examples.explanation: Returns the one matching order. The result verifies the query's logical behaviour separately from the plan description.

examples.title: Compare a selective filter with its result count
examples.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS review_orders FROM perf22_orders WHERE status = 'review';
examples.explanation: Counts the ten review orders. Whether a status index is useful depends on selectivity, table size and workload; the optimizer may reasonably scan a small table.

practise.guidedTask: Run the plan and result examples. Identify the predicate used for the primary-key search and explain why plan wording should not be hard-coded across SQLite versions.
practise.independentTask: Choose a query from a project, capture EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before and after adding a suitable index, verify identical results and record the observed plan differences.
hints: A plan describes an access strategy, not a guaranteed duration.
SCAN and SEARCH indicate different access approaches.
A primary key can support direct lookup.
Plan wording varies by engine version and statistics.
Verify results and measure representative data.

options: A description of how the engine intends to obtain query results
A backup of the database file
A list of all user passwords
questions.answer: A description of how the engine intends to obtain query results
questions.explanation: The optimizer selects an access and operation strategy for a query.

questions.prompt: What does SEARCH generally indicate in SQLite's query plan?
options: A constrained lookup that narrows the rows visited
questions.answer: A constrained lookup that narrows the rows visited
questions.explanation: SEARCH commonly indicates an indexed or otherwise constrained lookup.

questions.prompt: Does an index always make a query faster?
options: No; selectivity, table size and workload matter
Only when the table has no primary key
questions.answer: No; selectivity, table size and workload matter
questions.explanation: The optimizer may correctly choose a scan when it is cheaper.

questions.prompt: Why can EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN text change?
options: Engine version, schema, statistics and data can change the chosen plan
The table name is too short
questions.answer: Engine version, schema, statistics and data can change the chosen plan
questions.explanation: Plan output is diagnostic and should not be treated as a permanent string contract.

questions.prompt: What should accompany plan inspection during tuning?
options: Assuming the new plan is faster
questions.explanation: Tuning must preserve correctness and demonstrate performance on relevant workloads.
